    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 11:34 am CST.

    According to recent reports, david Beckham poses after he was made a knight bachelor at an investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle on Nov. 4, 2025, in Windsor, England. (Photo by Andrew Matthews/Getty Images).

    A German beauty group that makes and distributes former soccer player David Beckham’s fragrance line has kicked out at the soccer icon’s lawsuit against them, asking a New York court to dismiss the case.

    The Associated Press reported Tuesday that German-based Coty has argued that the Upcoming York Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction, and that Beckham’s commercial entity DB Ventures is simply using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from their deal to sign with another company.

    DB Ventures had originally filed suit in April, alleging that Beckham’s brand of luxury colognes and fragrances were being sold at gas stations and discount stores in violation of their agreement.

    According to the AP, Beckham’s name is a famous global brand synonymous with luxury and elegance.

    “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the complaint stated. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”.

    According to the AP, DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

    Sources indicate that coty told the AP that it strongly disputes the claims and would not comment further on ongoing litigation. Authentic Brands, DB Ventures’ parent tech giant, declined to comment to the AP.

    Beckham, a former Manchester United, Real Madrid, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain and LA Galaxy player who captained the English national football team and was knighted in 2025, has built a business career that includes co-owning soccer team Inter Miami.

    According to the Sunday Times, he is the first billionaire sports figure in the United Kingdom, having a combined net worth of about $1.58 billion with his wife, Victoria Beckham, a former member of the Spice Girls music group.

    • Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    Sources indicate that as the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it. There are important disputes tied to climate change, immigration, and the Second Amendment. But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs, birthright citizenship, executive authority, and the Voting Rights Act.

    Recent findings suggest that just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases. Perhaps of even greater note, though, is that it’s short on cases in general, as the court is running behind its typical pace for grants.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #8788. Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1575 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border.
    • The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.
    • Recent findings suggest that mullin v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

    The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

    Recent findings suggest that mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

    In a recent development, the Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be quickly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

    Sources indicate that the challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

    U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

    A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

    According to recent reports, judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”.

    Industry observers note that the D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

    In a recent development, contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most crucial and effective pieces of the President’s response.”.

    Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he noted, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”.

    Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”.

    And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent looks to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”.

    Industry observers note that the challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a upcoming removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”.

    In a recent development, the statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”.

    The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they mentioned, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

    The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

    Industry observers note that the court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services firm violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

    The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

    It has been revealed that the investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors mentioned, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”.

    Industry observers note that in a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the company’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”.

    The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”.

    The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    • Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 18, 2026, 12:42 pm CST.

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the state’s threshold for intoxication. (Image from Shutterstock).

    A judge in Michigan was found guilty Monday of drunk driving after he rear-ended a public transit bus, but a district court judge ruled that prosecutors failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his blood alcohol level met the threshold for the state’s original charge of a more serious offense.

    Warren 37th District Court Chief Judge John M. Chmura, 63, was found guilty of intoxication while driving his Ford Fusion into a parked bus that was displaying hazard lights March 25. But the court rejected the charge of Chmura driving with an elevated high blood alcohol content of 0.17 or greater, according to coverage on Law360.

    Novi 52nd District Court Judge David Law noted that Chmura’s judgment had been affected, but he questioned the blood alcohol concentration at the time of the crash.

    “This court may think it knows the answer to whether or not this was a high BAC case,” Law said. “But thinking it knows is not enough. It needs to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

    A bus driver sitting inside the bus waiting to resume his route was uninjured in the crash. Sterling Heights, Michigan, police officer Jonathan Journeau testified that Chmura smelled of alcohol, slurred his speech and couldn’t maintain his balance.

    Chmura’s attorney, David J. Kramer of the David J. Kramer Law Firm, argued that prosecutors could not establish the higher offense because Journeau failed to determine when the judge’s final alcoholic beverage was consumed.

    #8781. “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1339 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket.
    • Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice.
    • According to recent reports, in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “So Ordered.” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move promptly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he stated, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”.

    Sources indicate that readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

    The volume fell, but not to normal.

    According to recent reports, in the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

    Industry observers note that for most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump administration. Federal applications rose to eight in the 2018-19 term and nine in the 2019-20 term, then held at five or six a term under the Biden administration. In the 2024-25 term, the number jumped to a staggering 27.

    Against that record, the 2025-26 term’s 12 substantive applications from the executive branch are still the second-highest total in 26 years. The volume Alito described did fall. But it fell from an extraordinary peak to a level the court never saw before 2024.

    What “rival” means depends on what you count.

    The court resolved 123 emergency applications last term and decided 56 merits cases after full briefing and oral argument. By that measure, applications more than rival the merits cases.

    It has been revealed that but I would argue not every application belongs in that count. Forty-three of the 123 were refiled applications. Under the court’s Rule 22.4, an applicant denied by one justice may renew the request with another. The court denied all 43 refiled applications, and none drew a noted dissent. In fact, the court has not granted any of the 453 refiled applications it has resolved since 2000. Without refiles, the court resolved 80 applications last term.

    Another 44 were capital cases. The court has to rule on these, and they arrive on an execution timetable the court does not control. The court denied 42 of them. They take time, but they rarely divide the court.

    That leaves the 36 substantive applications, the ones that produce written opinions, noted dissents, and national consequences. Measured that way, the court decided 36 substantive applications and 56 merits cases.

    Alito’s explanation for the growth is specific. Presidents act by executive order, lower courts block those orders, and the government brings the fight to the Supreme Court.

    Recent findings suggest that as I explained above and elsewhere, the emergency docket has three different types of cases: capital cases, refiled applications, and substantive applications. Executive orders appear in only substantive applications. The four executive order applications make up 11% of the 36 substantive applications and 3% of all 123 applications the court resolved. None of the other 27 substantive applications involved an executive order. Redistricting alone accounted for 11 of them, more than the administration’s nine.

    The administration won five of the nine applications the court decided last term, or 56%. The term before it won 19 of 21. That 56% is the lowest win rate for any administration in the data. By comparison, the Trump administration won 77% of its applications in its first term, and the Biden administration won 63%.

    Pooled together, the two terms look ordinary. Adam Feldman’s recent analysis for SCOTUSblog found that the second Trump administration won 82% of the applications it brought through mid-October, close to its first-term rate. My data produce nearly the same pooled figure: 24 of 30, or 80%. This hides how things shifted: The administration won nearly every application in the 2024-25 term and barely more than half in the 2025-26 term.

    Specifically, the administration lost Trump v. Illinois, Blanche v. Perlmutter, Margolin v. National Association of Immigration Judges, and the Postal Service case. No justice noted a dissent in Margolin (though the administration later won the underlying dispute in May). Two of the four losses had ties to immigration: Illinois, over the National Guard deployment, and Margolin, over a policy limiting what immigration judges may say in public. But neither turned on immigration law itself. The administration won the one application that did, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., which allowed it to deport noncitizens to third-party countries. It went 2-1 in elections and 2-1 in executive power.

    It has been revealed that the 2024-25 term the court decided the administration’s applications in an average of 21 days, compared with 36 days for all other substantive applications. Last term the pattern reversed itself. The court took an average of 26 days on the administration’s applications and 15 days on everyone else’s. That 26-day average is the slowest for any administration in the data except the Bush administration, which filed only five applications.

    Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced term has followed the same pattern. Since Oct. 4, the court has decided three more administration applications and granted one, allowing border wall construction to resume in Texas. It denied the other two. One was the administration’s request, on the day before the midterm elections, to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. The court denied it in a one-line order, without asking California to respond and without a noted dissent. Counting from July, the administration has won two of its four election applications.

    In a recent development, alito predicted that the volume of emergency applications will continue to grow. A single term certainly cannot settle that question. And the administration keeps filing: It brought a cluster of election applications in the months before the midterms, filed again on the eve of the election, and has brought three applications to decision in the upcoming term.

    The 2025-26 term does show, however, how much the volume depends on a single litigant, in particular the executive. Indeed, the entire decline in substantive applications came from the executive branch. The administration asked the court for emergency relief less often, won less often, and waited longer for answers.

    According to recent reports, so Alito gets a mixed scorecard. He is right that the volume of such applications remains historically high: The executive branch’s 12 substantive applications are the second-highest total in 26 years, and the court resolved more applications than merits cases. The data cut against him on the source, though, at least last term: Only four of the administration’s 12 applications stemmed from executive orders. Finally, as to whether “this is going to continue,” one term does not make an era. The answer depends less on executive orders and more on the U.S. solicitor general’s office.

    The full numbers, including the justice-by-justice scorecard, the issue-area breakdown, and the complete term index, are in the 2025-26 Interim Relief Docket Stat Pack.

    According to recent reports, dr. Taraleigh Davis is an Assistant Professor of Public Law and American Politics at Bradley University.

    Recommended Citation: Taraleigh Davis, “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 16, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/im-afraid-this-is-going-to-continue-justice-alito-the-executive-and-the-emergency-docket/.

    #8778. Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Who supervises the system? Agentic AI and the future of lawyer oversight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer.
    • Systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps.
    • Recent findings suggest that the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Scott A. Meyers and Michael Adler.

    According to recent reports, for two years, the legal profession’s artificial intelligence conversation has centered on an attorney asking a system a question and checking its answer. That is no longer enough.

    Systems entering legal practice perform work: taking in a matter, researching, drafting motions, and choosing their own next steps. Used well, they can reduce routine work, freeing lawyers for judgment and client advice.

    Recent findings suggest that the profession built its supervision framework around people and bounded tools. An agentic system fits neither model: It has no license to lose or judgment to train, yet acts across a workflow with autonomy the Model Rules do not squarely address.

    When AI moves from answering questions to executing multistep legal workflows, what does meaningful human oversight look like?

    The unit of supervision is no longer an answer; it is a system of delegated decisions.

    Sources indicate that the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct anticipated part of this shift. In 2012, the ABA changed Rule 5.3’s title from “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistants” to “Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance.” Its comments encompassed technology-enabled services; a companion resolution added technological competence to what became Comment 8 of Rule 1.1. In 2024, Formal Opinion 512 applied Rules 1.1, 5.1, and 5.3 to lawyers’ use of generative AI and their supervision of the people and providers using it.

    According to recent reports, that guidance remains organized around a tool: review its output, protect client information, train customers and assess providers. It offers less direction when the system executes the workflow, deciding which documents to pull, which facts matter, and what goes where—decisions the finished product may not reveal. Reviewing only the output confirms the car arrived, not its route. Supervision of output is not supervision of process.

    Industry observers note that METR’s May 2026 report sharpens the point. Assessing agents inside frontier developers (or entities that train AI models), it found them exceeding intended bounds and misleading users about their work, especially on difficult tasks. It did not study law firm deployments, and routine monitoring might have caught every incident because an independent record existed. The lesson: A lawyer cannot treat an agent’s account as the record of its work. That account is another output of the same probabilistic process, which has training incentives that can reward telling users what they want to hear. Asking the agent to double-check itself is not an independent control.

    It has been revealed that accountability cannot rest solely with whoever pressed “run.” It must be institutional and individual, extending to those who designed, approved and maintained the workflow. Every deployed workflow should have a named lawyer-owner authorized to pause it, just as every matter has a responsible partner. This does not displace the matter lawyer’s responsibilities. The owner’s authority must permit suspension on suspicion alone before a committee convenes or a vendor responds. Ownership without it is a label.

    Final output review remains necessary. Oversight must also cover consequential junctures: privilege calls, external communications, filings and anything irreversible or beyond client authorization. Supervision begins at design time: deciding what a workflow may do independently, its latitude to reason, and where it must stop and ask. Every firm should be able to answer: Where can this system act without a human seeing it first, and who decided that?

    It has been revealed that A tested record on comparable work can justify less intensive routine checking, though never at those consequential junctures. Greater autonomy should be approved and recorded. Material changes to the model, tools, permissions or workflow should trigger reassessment and renewed authorization.

    Autonomy bundles three permissions requiring separate calibration: generating work product, accessing sensitive information, and acting in firm or client systems. Permissions should narrow as consequences grow: broad room to draft; matter-scoped room to read; and narrow, logged room to act. A first-year may draft the memo; nobody gives them unilateral wire authority. The grant of action is never implied by the grant of access.

    If a firm cannot trace what a system did, it cannot supervise it; where reasoning cannot be audited, behavior must be. Otherwise, recordkeeping, preservation, and verification of representations to clients, courts, and third parties may suffer. Three mechanisms matter: an audit trail independent of the agent’s reporting, means to interrupt workflows mid-run, and a path to unwind reversible actions—with honesty about those that cannot be reversed. Record model versions and configurations too: Providers upgrade continuously, and a workflow validated in March may differ from August’s.

    Five workflows can be governed individually; 500 cannot. Solo and small practices may use a simple inventory but still need a way to stop a workflow. At scale, governance becomes operational infrastructure: an inventory of deployed systems, risk classification, approval gates, monitoring and reassessment. The profession knows this playbook: Ask a managing partner how conflicts are governed, and you will hear about a system, not a policy.

    According to recent reports, delay accumulates governance debt: workflows deployed faster than they can be inventoried, permissions granted faster than they can be reviewed. Like all debt, it compounds quietly. When data-protection regimes preceded settled enforcement guidance, prudent organizations built from regulatory intent rather than waiting for caselaw. Agentic AI presents the same problem: established duties but no settled operating model.

    Ownership, calibrated oversight, permission limits, traceability, reversibility and governance at scale matter wherever organizations deploy agentic AI. What distinguishes law is that our supervisory duties are explicit and long-standing. We are not a special case. We are an early test case.

    It has been revealed that fortunately, the test is familiar. Lawyers have been supervising work they did not personally perform since the first associate billed their first hour. The question is no longer only whether lawyers can use AI competently. It is whether we can supervise systems that increasingly do the work of the supervised.

    In a recent development, scott A. Meyers is the chairman and CEO, and Michael Adler is the director of artificial intelligence governance and data protection at Akerman, an Am Law 100 law firm.

    #8776. Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1858 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Listening to the past

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is.
    • In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians.
    • A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

    In a recent development, in a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded, but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

    A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

    The role of history in text-and-history cases.

    Sources indicate that originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

    According to recent reports, sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary definition of the Constitution’s words. Sometimes, it is necessary to look to history to understand what those words did, legally speaking.

    For example, it is relatively easy to understand the opening words of Article III: “The judicial Power of the United States, shall be vested in one supreme Court, and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.” But what is the significance of the decision to give the “judicial Power of the United States” to Article III courts and not, say, to “the executive Departments”? The answer to that question is not to be found exclusively in a dictionary definition of “judicial Power.” It is to be found in historical sources revealing what, in 1789, the “judicial Power” enabled an actor to do. Whatever that is, Article III courts can do it, and an executive department cannot.

    Similarly, the Second Amendment guarantees that “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” But we know that that right has always been understood to coexist with some limited forms of regulation. We will not necessarily be able to figure out what forms of regulation are permissible just by looking at how “right” and “infringed” were used in old dictionaries. Courts must uncover a more complex historical idea.

    Sources indicate that that is why 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen, an originalist opinion in which the court held that New York’s concealed carry law was inconsistent with the Second Amendment, requires courts adjudicating Second Amendment challenges to move past the text to look at history: namely, “the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” If the government can prove that its firearms regulation fits the history, then the government may prevail even though it seeks to restrict the right described in the text.

    One consequence of the Bruen methodology is that, if the government cannot find a historical regulation that resembles its modern regulation, then it may lose. This is a problem, critics argue, because there are plenty of reasons the legislatures of the past might have chosen not to regulate in a particular way.

    Sources indicate that for example, the founding generation did not disarm casual users of intoxicating substances. One reason may be that they believed such a regulation would infringe the right to keep and bear arms. An early refusal to regulate on that ground would then provide good evidence that the right was originally understood to foreclose the would-be regulation. But there are other possibilities: the regulation would have been inexpedient, impolitic, unnecessary. Or perhaps it just never occurred to the legislators.

    If the government cannot fit its modern regulation into the historical regulatory tradition, then the modern regulation fails Bruen’s test. Thus, Bruen does not distinguish these sources of silence. It seems to draw the same inference from them: unconstitutionality.

    Industry observers note that this criticism – that the lack of a historical regulatory tradition doesn’t tell you very much – is misplaced for several reasons. First, historical legislatures legislated against a background common-law tradition that included robust principles concerning appropriate firearm regulation, even if those principles weren’t spelled out in legislation. The common-law practices on which the court relied in, say, United States v. Rahimi (in which it upheld a federal law disarming persons under a domestic violence restraining order) are part of that tradition and reveal a baseline principle: the state may act on demonstrated or threatened misuse of firearms by individuals. Legislative silence was not regulatory silence – the common law hummed on.

    Industry observers note that second, and relatedly, courts do not treat historical regulations as “molds” into which modern legislators must pour their regulatory ambitions. Rather, as Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained in her concurrence in Rahimi, the historical inquiry “demands a wider lens: Historical regulations reveal a principle, not a mold.” Principles convert some silences into spaces for modern regulatory innovation: firearms laws that differ in detail, but not in principle, from their predecessors. Conversely, if no historical regulation anywhere, anytime reflects the principle animating a restriction on someone’s ability to keep and bear arms (as was the case in last term’s decision rejecting a federal attempt to disarm someone based on casual drug use in United States v. Hemani), then that “silence” speaks more eloquently than originalism’s critics imagine.

    It has been revealed that finally, and most key in my view, the criticism mistakes the role of the historical inquiry in Second Amendment adjudications. The text of the Second Amendment is the first and best evidence of its meaning, and it is always speaking. Bruen directs courts to begin with the text and turn to history only after concluding that the regulation implicates the Second Amendment. Before a court ever turns to the “historical tradition of firearm regulation,” then, it has already concluded that the government is restricting someone’s ability to keep and bear arms. To the extent that silences in the historical record create doubt about whether that restriction is permissible or impermissible, the textual analysis justifies shifting the burden of that uncertainty onto the government. The government has failed to justify restricting what the Constitution describes as protected conduct. Tie goes to the rights-holder.

    Sources indicate that sometimes, judges face the opposite problem: not silence, but too much noise. Professor Rachel Bayefsky wrote last week about seemingly dissonant traditions at play in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, a case in which the court heard argument on Nov. 10.

    Sources indicate that sun Valley involves an appeal from a Department of Labor enforcement action imposing penalties on Sun Valley Orchards for breaching work contracts with foreign laborers brought into the country under the H-2A visa program. The court must decide whether that enforcement action, which the department both prosecuted and adjudicated, belongs instead in an Article III court.

    According to recent reports, recall that only Article III courts hold “the judicial Power of the United States.” History reveals that the government needs the “judicial Power” to deprive someone – like Sun Valley Orchards – of a private right, like property. But it does not need to exercise judicial power to exercise a sovereign (or so-called “public”) right, like the right to decide who enters the country, or to confer a privilege, like a visa. To put it a little more simply: If the government wants to take money that is already in your bank account, then it must take you to court. If you want the government to pay you money that is in the Treasury, then the government can handle your request “in house” (i.e., in the agency charged with administering the benefits scheme).

    Bayefsky describes these as competing traditions brought into conflict by the parties’ claims: Sun Valley invokes its private right to the money the department seeks to collect from it; the department brandishes its sovereign power and the conditions it attached to the privilege of hiring foreign laborers. Bayefsky suggests that the conflict creates an indeterminacy, which the court might resolve by turning to considerations other than text and history to reach a conclusion about what the Constitution requires today.

    Many voices, like silences, present a challenge to originalism. But varied traditions do not foreclose determinacy, any more than polyphony forecloses harmony. Sometimes, as in Sun Valley, the traditions proceed in counterpoint.

    It has been revealed that from an originalist perspective, the history at the heart of Sun Valley reflects a single, coherent constitutional rule: When the executive wants to take away someone’s private property, it must go to court. It follows that when the executive wants to do something that does not involve taking away someone’s private property (or life or liberty), it need not go to court. But the mere existence of sovereign interests or privileges does not justify taking a private-rights case out of court.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, it is possible for the Constitution to point one way, while more recent traditions point another. That is what creates the puzzle Bayefsky is writing about: Historical traditions reflecting the original meaning of the Constitution required Article III adjudications for private-rights deprivations. More recent traditions reflecting a compromise with the demands of modern government permit agency adjudication when sovereign interests are at stake. These traditions conflict when a private-rights case implicates sovereign interests. When that happens, as Bayefsky says, courts must decide: which tradition?

    Recent findings suggest that the existence of competing traditions is one reason to prefer an originalist text-and-history method to a non-originalist history-and-tradition method (as I have written in a previous column). Originalism’s answer to “which tradition” is, in a way, “neither.” Its objective is not to follow a tradition, but instead to discern the legal rule created by the Constitution, which history can reveal. While it may not be easy to know into which category the rights at problem in Sun Valley fall, the court is looking for a single answer, at a single point in time. The law supplies that single answer. The judge’s challenge is to sort through the admittedly conflicting evidence to decide which side has the best account of it.

    Of course, a judge listening for original meaning may hear complex, interlaced melodies – and even the occasional sour note – but he is more likely to find harmony in text and history than in tradition.

    Haley Proctor is an Associate Professor at Notre Dame Law School, where she researches and teaches about procedure, evidence, and the judicial system.

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re seeking a Technical Account Manager (TAM) to be the primary technical partner for our Team & customers after the sale, helping them adopt, operate, and get long-term value from Supabase.

    At Supabase, TAMs are the technical owners of their assigned accounts, working closely with our most valuable customers to:.

    Understand each customer’s architecture, use cases, constraints, and goals.

    Validate deployments and guide customers through onboarding and early success.

    Proactively surface risks and optimization opportunities before they become incidents.

    Coordinate internal teams on complex escalations and drive root cause analysis.

    Align Supabase capabilities with the customer’s roadmap.

    Successful TAMs are proactive, technically credible, and customer-first. TAM is a relationship, not a response channel: you’ll act as an extension of your customers’ teams and advocate on their behalf within Supabase.

    You’ll be joining our Success team, where you will be expected to lead and innovate around the following areas of responsibility:.

    Technical Ownership & Onboarding.

    Act as the technical owner for your assigned accounts, documenting environments, mapping dependencies, and tracking technical risks.

    Validate architecture and deployment intends after the sale, guide initial configuration and best practices, and make sure customers understand platform capabilities and limitations.

    Help customers reach early success milestones to shorten time to value and reduce early friction.

    Regularly review customer environments and usage patterns to identify scalability, performance, reliability, security, and compliance risks and opportunities.

    Strategy upgrades and lifecycle events, and run architecture reviews for upcoming initiatives, including capacity and growth planning, feature readiness, and early identification of technical blockers.

    Coordinate across Support and Engineering on complex or high-impact issues. TAMs are not frontline support, but provide the context, prioritization, and follow-through that drive resolution, root cause analysis, and preventative action.

    Serve as the voice of the customer to Engineering and Product, sharing specific, reproducible feedback on recurring pain points and taking part in beta and early access programs.

    Partner with Sales and Customer Success on account health and retention, with technical input on renewals, expansions, and evaluations, and early flags on risks to satisfaction.

    6+ years of relevant work experience in engineering, SRE, technical consulting, or similar, including operating production systems under real constraints.

    Sources indicate that strong technical depth across database internals, scalability, security posture, and infrastructure tradeoffs. You understand a customer’s architecture as well as they do, without escalating every question.

    A proactive mindset: you spot risks and optimization opportunities before the customer does, and you treat your accounts like a personal portfolio.

    Sound escalation judgment: you know when to escalate, when to resolve internally, and how to communicate clearly under pressure without creating noise.

    Recent findings suggest that very strong communication skills. TAMs explain complex issues to non-technical executives and root causes to senior engineers, often in the same day.

    Awareness of how TAM performance shows up in retention and NRR, including surfacing expansion signals and renewal risks early.

    Experience working in async or globally distributed teams.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire tech giant gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    It has been revealed that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    Recent findings suggest that we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    A Ninth Circuit panel questioned whether DHS regulations prohibiting loud or unusual noise near federal buildings give officers too much discretion to restrict protests.

    Recent findings suggest that (CN) âÂ On the inside of a federal building in Eugene, Oregon, IRS workers interviewed taxpayers. On the outside, protesters blared megaphones in opposition to the Trump administrationâs immigration policies.

    In a recent development, the government called it a disruption. The protesters called it free speech.

    A federal judge in Oregon blocked the Trump administration earlier this year from enforcing new regulations that prohibited protesters from making unusual noise at federal buildings that could disrupt workers. But the government was back in court Thursday to ask a Ninth Circuit panel to reverse that order.

    âThe regulatory provision at glitch in this case reflects the common sense notion that loud or unusual noise emanating from right outside a federal building can disrupt government operations, just as loud or unusual noise inside the building can,â Department of Justice attorney Brian Springer told a three-judge panel. âThese sorts of noise restrictions are long-standing and prevalent throughout the law.â.

    The lower court had found the upcoming regulation on noise was too vague under the Fifth Amendmentâs due process clause, but Springer countered that, saying “the Supreme Court, this court and federal courts of appeals across the country have repeatedly and consistently upheld similar provisions against vagueness challenges like the one here, because the language affords fair notice about what conduct is covered.”.

    However, Springer met resistance from all three members of the panel, all Joe Biden appointees, who questioned the governmentâs citation of related cases in its opening brief, as well as its use of language in the regulations prohibiting unusual noise.

    âI think anyone would appreciate that the megaphone use at issue here was precisely the type of activity that would be likely to affect people working inside this office building,â Springer told the panel.

    But the judges also questioned how much discretion federal officers would have to enforce the regulations and whether the regulations could apply in different types of federal buildings.

    Sources indicate that âWhat if it’s next to a busy street?" U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung asked. “There’s a traffic jam, someone starts honking, people inside the federal building can hear it, they seem to be affected by a loud or unusual noise. Would that subject them? Would that be a violation?â.

    Springer noted the noise has to actually affect the operations of the building.

    âThat’s exactly the question, and you’re not answering it, so I’m really interested in whether the answer is yes or no,â U.S. Circuit Judge Roopali Desai mentioned. âIf it could affect the operations of an individual inside the federal building, would it be a violation of this regulation? And if the answer is no, why not?â.

    It depends, Springer stated, adding âI think a fleeting honk is very unlikely to violate the regulation.â.

    In a recent development, âIt’s loud or unusual noise in areas outside of property that affects persons on the federal property,â Sung continued. âSo if I can hear it, and it’s loud, why isn’t that affecting me?â.

    âYour honor, the sorts of affects that the agency is looking for are the ones that we have in this case, where plaintiffs were using ââ.

    In a recent development, âBut you need something in the regulation that narrows it to those ‘affects,’â Sung interrupted. âWhat is the plain meaning of âaffectâ? Because normally, I think, in plain meaning, affect has a very broad meaning.â.

    Marianne Dugan, representing the protesters who sued after the regulations were issued, argued that the exchange with the government attorney illustrated why the regulation was facially unconstitutional and could not be narrowed.

    It has been revealed that âYou have this word âaffects,â which gives almost total discretion to anybody reading it who’s enforcing that rule to say, âYour noise is affecting the people in this building,ââ said Dugan, an attorney with the Eugene-based Civil Liberties Defense Center. âThe district court’s factual findings are not clearly erroneous, its conclusions of law were legally correct and the scope of the injunction is not an abuse of discretion.".

    Industry observers note that the regulation has a chilling effect on ordinary people who want to protest at federal buildings, she remarked. Despite the preliminary injunction, a protester was threatened as recently as Wednesday with a citation, she added.

    The protesters filed their lawsuit in December 2025, after they were cited and arrested for violating the regulations that went into affect the previous month. They are seeking a permanent injunction of the regulation.

    The protesters have established regular protests outside of the Eugene federal building, which is next to the office for Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

    #8771. Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Supreme Court turns down DEI-related disputes and Second Amendment challenge to gun bans in “sensitive places”

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.
    • The court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v.
    • Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    The court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    The research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    In a recent development, thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    In a recent development, in June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    Sources indicate that the Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    In a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    In their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Sources indicate that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    In a recent development, khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    After the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they said, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    The Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the issue at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    In a recent development, thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    In a recent development, in rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    It has been revealed that maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at issue in this case, the state stated, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    In his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    Strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At issue in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    And in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    Sources indicate that in its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Upcoming York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    The United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    Recent findings suggest that justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    âHow can the system survive if the general public thinks that judges have skin in the game?â asked one judge on the New York Court of Appeals.

    (CN) â In 2023, defendant Glaston Gaines was given a choice: face up to 25 years in prison for a robbery charge or plead guilty and waive his right to appeal in exchange for a sentencing commitment of 10 to 13 years from the trial judge.

    Industry observers note that he chose the latter, and was ultimately sentenced to 12 years in prison for his role in the crime. But the maneuver from the judge was under the microscope of the New York Court of Appeals on Thursday, as the seven-judge panel grappled with whether court-initiated appeal waivers should be lawful at all.

    Industry observers note that gaines claims they arenât. His lawyer, Legal Aid attorney Sarod Nori, told the stateâs high court that these waivers are âa threat to the legitimacy of the criminal justice system,â since it amounts to coercion from the trial judge â who is supposed to be impartial.

    In Gainesâ case, the appeal waiver wasnât part of his plea deal with the prosecution at all. Instead, it was tacked on as an added requirement from the court in exchange for the commitment to the sentencing time range.

    âA sentence is not a bargaining chip that a judge can use,â Nori argued.

    What ensued was a debate over the intended purpose of a court-initiated appeal waiver in the first place. Nori suggested they are an option for judges âin the interest of finality,â so criminal cases can be closed without victims having to reopen old wounds in the appellate process. Judge Madeline Singas brought up a hypothetical of a 9-year-old rape victim, whom a judge might want to protect from the proceedings by offering such a waiver agreement for sentencing.

    Chief Judge Rowan Wilson took it a different way.

    In a recent development, âThe reason we have appeal waivers is so the system doesnât get flooded with cases we canât try because there’s too many of them,â he said. âItâs really an efficiency point, no?â.

    Either way, Nori maintained itâs an unlawful tool in the trial courtâs belt. According to court filings, Gaines told his judge, âI feel like I have no choiceâ but to accept the appeal waiver when he pleaded guilty. He was also denied the opportunity to speak at his plea hearing after the judge told him to save it for sentencing.

    Even the state admitted that may have been a misstep.

    âI will concede that if the defendant is asking to say something, that the judge should probably allow him to say it,â state attorney April Orlowski told the court Thursday.

    Judge Michael Garcia suggested these concerns could just be handled on a case-by-case basis by the appellate division. While an appeal waiver generally prevents a defendant from appealing most aspects of their conviction and sentence, they can still make a challenge if the deal itself was made in bad faith â as Gaines claims his was.

    The court didnât immediately issue a ruling following the hearing. But several of its judges offered up critiques about the optics of greenlighting the practice. Judge Caitlin Halligan said it could lead to an appearance of bias for a judge since it âinsulatesâ their decision from further review.

    Judge Jenny Rivera expressed similar concerns.

    âHow can the system survive if the general public thinks that judges have skin in the game, that theyâre interested in a particular outcome, that theyâre seeking favoritism for one side over the other?â she asked.

    Industry observers note that laws surrounding court-initiated appeal waivers vary from state to state. Newly introduced York has taken a nuanced approach to the matter, defined largely by a 1989 ruling in *People v. Seaberg,*which found that a defendant can indeed waive their appellate rights in exchange for a more favorable sentence from the court. But earlier this year in People v. Turner, a mid-level state appellate court found that the trial court must provide an on-the-record rationale for their appeal waiver.
