    #8744. Five major concerns that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2653 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Five major concerns that may still make it onto this term’s oral argument docket

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket.
    • But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review.
    • In a recent development, before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Under the Supreme Court’s typical briefing schedule, a case must be granted by mid-January to be briefed in time for the final argument session, which begins this term on April 19.

    But despite being short on time, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile complications as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers, state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms, and the regulation of prediction markets like Kalshi.

    In a recent development, before we explore some of the major issues pending before the Supreme Court, let me first offer a brief refresher on how a petition for review makes it to the oral argument docket. (For more on this process, read law professor Stephen Wermiel’s SCOTUSblog column from last week.).

    It has been revealed that litigants file a petition for review, also known as a petition for certiorari, at the Supreme Court when they want the justices to review a lower court ruling against them. In their petition, they lay out, among other things, their views on why the ruling was wrong and why the concern is worthy of the justices’ attention.

    Sources indicate that after a petition is filed, the litigants that prevailed before the lower court (known as the respondents) have 30 days to respond, although they may ask for additional time. Sometimes, they file a brief in which they agree that the Supreme Court should take up the issue, but it’s far more common for respondents to file a brief in opposition, in which they explain why they believe the lower court’s ruling was correct and why the dispute does not warrant Supreme Court review.

    Once this brief has been filed – or once the respondent has formally waived its right to file such a brief (although the court may request one) – the court will schedule the petition for consideration at one of the justices’ private conferences. There are at least two such conferences every month during the term, and the court announces in advance when these meetings will take place and when it will distribute the petitions assigned to each conference to the justices’ chambers.

    The court typically places a petition on a conference list at least 14 days after the response brief was filed. By counting 14 days from the response deadline and then consulting the distribution schedule, one can then (usually) predict the conference at which the justices will first consider a petition. (It should be noted, however, that the court sometimes delays consideration of a petition without explanation, interfering with court watchers’ predictive powers.).

    Sources indicate that for a petition to make it to the oral argument docket, at least four of the nine justices need to vote to grant review. But the court rarely unveils that a petition has been granted after the first conference at which it’s considered, likely because the court needs extra time to verify the details of the case. Instead, successful petitions are almost always relisted at least once, which means the justices take a second look at them during a successive conference. For this reason, the earliest a court watcher can expect to learn that a petition has been granted is generally after the second conference to which it’s assigned.

    According to recent reports, once a case is granted, litigants must file briefs on the merits, a process that takes at least three months under the court’s standard briefing schedule. That’s why a case must be granted by mid-January in order to be argued during the current term (unless the court adopts an expedited briefing schedule, which is a story for another day).

    Without further ado, here’s a look at five high-profile concerns that have a shot at being taken up by the justices before that mid-January deadline.

    Ban on transgender servicemembers.

    One week after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he signed an executive order that required Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to impose a ban “on individuals with gender dysphoria” – that is, distress based on a mismatch between an individual’s gender identity and biological sex. The next month, the Department of Defense issued a policy that generally disqualifies anyone who either has gender dysphoria or has undergone medical interventions to treat gender dysphoria from serving in the military.

    This ban on transgender servicemembers led to a number of legal challenges, including a dispute that arrived on the Supreme Court’s interim docket in April 2025, United States v. Shilling. On May 6, 2025, the court granted the Trump administration’s request to pause an order from a federal judge in Washington state that had prevented implementation of the policy anywhere in the country.

    Shilling is now pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit. A separate but related case, United States v. Talbott, has been appealed to the Supreme Court. Talbott involves a group of transgender people who either presently serve or want to serve in the U.S. military. After the Trump administration put the service ban in place, they went to federal court in Washington, D.C., contending that the policy violates their constitutional right to equal treatment by the government.

    In March 2025, a federal judge in D.C. granted the challengers’ request to put the policy on hold, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of the district court’s order in a June 2026 ruling, deciding that, while the case is ongoing, the Trump administration may not enforce its ban against the 28 current servicemembers involved. (However, the D.C. Circuit did not finalize that ruling until this week, after considering arguments over whether it should be implemented during the government’s appeal.).

    U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed the D.C. Circuit’s ruling to the Supreme Court in late August, urging the justices to address the constitutionality of the ban on transgender servicemembers. He described the lower court decision as “gravely erroneous” and asserted that “[t]he authority of the U.S. military to determine who may serve in the Nation’s armed forces is a matter of exceptional importance.”.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 2, the challengers filed their brief in opposition and encouraged the Supreme Court to deny the petition. They emphasized that the D.C. Circuit issued a narrow preliminary injunction, not a broad final judgment, and that the record below is not yet developed.

    Industry observers note that as expected under the timeline discussed above, this petition was included on the conference list that was distributed on Tuesday, for the justices’ private conference on Dec. 4. If Talbott is relisted after the Dec. 4 conference, it will be considered again on Dec. 11 and could possibly be granted that day.

    Recent findings suggest that this week marks 46 years since the Supreme Court in Stone v. Graham struck down a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms, holding that the law violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause. The justices have an opportunity to revisit that 1980 ruling this term if they take up challenges to similar policies in Texas and Louisiana.

    Nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District is a challenge to the Texas law by a group of families with children in the state’s public schools. They contend that, in upholding the law, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit “flouted this Court’s binding precedents and gutted the religious-freedom rights of public-school children and parents.”.

    Sources indicate that last week, Texas filed a brief in opposition to the petition, urging the justices to leave the 5th Circuit’s ruling in place. Among other arguments, the state notes that Texas’ incoming Democratic attorney general “has publicly stated that he ‘will not defend’ the challenged law” and contends that the issue will benefit from “further percolation in the lower courts.”.

    In addition to upholding Texas’ law, the 5th Circuit vacated preliminary injunctions preventing implementation of a similar policy in Louisiana. Despite this win, Louisiana filed a “conditional petition” with the Supreme Court in Brumley v. Roake, anticipating that the ACLU, which represents the challengers in both the Texas and Louisiana cases, would only appeal Nathan and telling the court that it should not review Texas’ law without also considering Louisiana’s law.

    Industry observers note that in a separate case, Dier v. Landry, a Louisiana teacher, Christopher Dier, also asked the justices to consider whether Louisiana’s policy violates the establishment clause, but his case is complicated by a question of whether the fact that he filed his challenge before the law was implemented means it was not “ripe.” In its brief in opposition, Louisiana repeated the arguments it made in its conditional petition in Roake, asserting that the justices should grant one or both of the Louisiana cases if it grants review in the Texas case.

    According to recent reports, because Texas’ response in Nathan and Louisiana’s response in Dier were filed on Nov. 10, these petitions will likely be considered by the justices for the first time at their Dec. 11 conference. That is the second and final conference in December, so it will be early January before the petitions could be considered a second time and potentially granted.

    As I previously reported for SCOTUSblog, immigration issues dominate this term’s oral argument docket. The court is weighing, among other things, the Trump administration’s practice of deporting noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders, its policy of detaining noncitizens without the opportunity for bond hearings, and its suspension of asylum.

    And there may be more immigration disputes to come. The justices are expected to soon consider Trump v. Suri and Khalil v. Trump, which address federal trial courts’ authority to review the legality of immigration detentions.

    Sources indicate that suri and Khalil, which involve Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri and Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil, respectively, stem from the Trump administration’s push to deport students and academics because of their support for Palestine. Suri and Khalil were detained as part of this push, and while their deportation proceedings were ongoing, they challenged the legality of their detention in federal trial courts, alleging First Amendment violations. Both men prevailed before district courts, which ordered their release on bail. But while the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld the decision in Suri’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that the district court did not have the authority to consider Khalil’s challenges.

    Both cases have now been appealed to the Supreme Court, and they raise essentially the same question: Do federal trial courts have the power to consider a noncitizen’s challenge to his or her detention, or are such claims barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court? In the government’s petition in Suri, Sauer told the justices that it may be best to grant review in both cases, because that approach “would guard against the possibility that either case might become moot (for example, due to the alien’s departure).”.

    According to recent reports, the responses to these petitions are due on Friday. The court’s case distribution schedule indicates that they likely will be considered by the justices for the first time at their private conference on Jan. 8.

    Regulation of prediction markets.

    According to recent reports, the rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket has fueled a fierce legal battle between the companies operating the markets, state gambling regulators, and the federal government. The question at the center of the dispute is whether the prediction markets are subject to state gambling laws, or if, instead, they should answer only to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that regulates contract markets.

    In a recent development, several federal courts of appeals have ruled on this question in recent months, and others are currently considering it. In Flaherty v. KalshiEX, LLC, Upcoming Jersey asks the Supreme Court to review a 3rd Circuit ruling in favor of Kalshi, which bars the state from enforcing gambling laws against the company. Robinhood Derivatives, LLC v. Dreitzer and North American Derivatives Exchange, Inc., dba Crypto.com v. Nevada are appeals of rulings by the 9th Circuit that reached the opposite conclusion: that contracts offered by prediction markets are not “swaps” and that, as a result, the CFTC does not have an exclusive right to regulate them.

    All of the parties involved agree that the stakes are high, urging the Supreme Court to get involved now and bring a resolution to the still-building surge of litigation.

    Sources indicate that the responses to these three prediction market petitions are due on Dec. 7. The cases will likely then be distributed to the justices for consideration at the Jan. 8 conference.

    Judicial authority and other Trump cases.

    In its June 2025 ruling in Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court held that federal courts generally lack the authority to issue universal or nationwide injunctions blocking the government from enforcing a law or policy anywhere in the country. The ruling was significant, but it did not necessarily foreclose all forms of broad relief, as the Trump administration makes clear in Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, a petition it filed in October.

    Sources indicate that after CASA, lower courts have continued “to universally vacate agency rules under the Administrative Procedure Act,” the federal law governing administrative agencies, according to the petition. In so doing, Sauer wrote, they “re-create many of the same problems posed by universal injunctions.” He urged the justices to take up Texas Medical Association and “return the lower courts to their proper role under the APA” by making it clear “that relief should ordinarily be party-specific, not universal by default.”.

    In a recent development, the case began as a group of challenges from the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies to a 2022 law aimed at protecting patients from surprise medical bills. These challengers have until Dec. 14 to respond to the Trump administration’s petition.

    That deadline means this petition likely won’t be considered by the justices until their Jan. 15 conference at the earliest. As noted above, cases typically need to be granted by mid-January to be argued during the current term, although the court sometimes adjusts the standard briefing schedule if it wants to add cases after the typical cut-off. The bottom line is that Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association faces a steeper path to this term’s oral argument docket than the previously discussed petitions.

    It has been revealed that the justices are also expected to address several other notable filings involving Trump by mid-January, including cases involving the president’s attempt to revive his suit against Hillary Clinton over what he describes as “a coordinated scheme ... to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion”; Trump’s suit against CNN for, according to him, “falsely and maliciously portray[ing]” him “as a knowing liar” with regard to the 2020 election; and his appeal of a $83.3 million judgment against him in a defamation case brought by journalist E. Jean Carroll.

    While it may be difficult to predict which disputes will make it to the oral argument docket, it’s not hard to conclude that the justices are in for a busy two months.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #8741. Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1331 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Calls for court packing fail the test of history

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify.
    • According to recent reports, some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton said the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

    According to recent reports, some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

    It is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

    So how can one tell the difference?

    It has been revealed that as we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

    Political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

    Recent findings suggest that the 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each upcoming circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

    But circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

    Sources indicate that timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

    It has been revealed that to clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This demonstrates, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

    Industry observers note that finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

    Recent findings suggest that the allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”.

    According to recent reports, jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Among social media ads, short-form video drives the most actions

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal.
    • In a recent development, doubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific.
    • Recent findings suggest that those people are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech firm DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook — and their respective short-form formats — as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.

    In a recent development, doubleVerify compiled its report by collecting responses from 22,000 consumers and 2,020 marketers, spanning regions like North America, Latin America, EMEA, and Asia-Pacific. One thing those global respondents can agree on is their appreciation of YouTube. Google’s video hub is the most-used platform across all age groups and regions, with 95% of all respondents claiming to use it.

    Recent findings suggest that those people are also warming up to YouTube’s ad ecosystem. Half of the respondents remarked they would take action based on YouTube ads; that was the highest percentage among all measured platforms. Facebook came in second on that axis (49%), followed by Instagram (42%) and TikTok (38%).

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, other platforms are lagging behind in terms of actionable ads, and DoubleVerify’s findings suggest a significant difference between those four industry leaders and their competitors. YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok are four platforms where short-form media has been widely adopted, and 38% of DoubleVerify respondents mentioned that short-form ads inspire them to take action. That was 7% higher than the next ad format on the list (long-form video pre-rolls, at 31%).

    The ubiquity of short-form video is one factor that seems to be making ads more palatable across social media. Since the release of DoubleVerify’s 2025 Global Insights Report, 8% more consumers have decided that social media platforms are suitable locations for ads. YouTube, at 72%, was deemed the most valid platform for those spots.

    DoubleVerify’s report reveals that social media spend is paying off across multiple platforms, but marketers must still pick and choose as they allocate their ad dollars. As we saw with the Pew Research Center’s recent survey of American social media habits, usage data can vary wildly depending on demographic filters like age, gender, and household income.

    That assertion held true in the DoubleVerify report, in which TikTok ranked as the third most-used platform among 18-to-24-year-olds but didn’t crack the top five among the 65+ set. And most platforms skewed male worldwide, but 8% more female respondents use Pinterest compared to men.

    It has been revealed that the global scope of DoubleVerify’s report adds another wrinkle to the conversation. In the Asia-Pacific region, for example, 56% of respondents said that influencer activity “somewhat to significantly” impacted purchase decisions. In North America, that statistic is only 39%. So if marketers want to ensure that their social media activity inspires action, they should deploy their budgets wisely.

    Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 18; updated with latest developments on Nov.
    • The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon.
    • It has been revealed that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

    The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”.

    It has been revealed that then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he unveiled that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

    Sources indicate that after Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, revealed her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

    In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

    When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it issues a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a latest lower-court ruling.

    Finally, a few housekeeping notes:.

    On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

    Also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

    On Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

    Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

    In a recent development, the December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Michael Phillis, Associated Press.

    In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and mentioned the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”.

    Nicholas Kristof, The Latest York Times.

    According to recent reports, in a column for The New York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

    Sources indicate that in a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

    Industry observers note that in a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” remarked Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”.

    In a recent development, on Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”.

    Sources indicate that time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

    Sources indicate that by Jordan J. Ballor & Logan Tantibanchachai.

    In a recent development, in a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan J. Ballor and Logan Tantibanchachai reflected on Democrats’ recent embrace of court packing, which they “define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.” Such an approach to court reform “risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently,” they wrote.

    By César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández.

    In his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored what Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could mean for a challenge to an Iowa law criminalizing certain immigration-related conduct, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Because Iowa’s Republican attorney general lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, it’s now unclear if the state will move forward with its defense of the law, “providing yet another reason why elections matter.”.

    In a recent development, in his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky revisited the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, during which several conservative justices appeared to suggest “that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.” Such an approach to free exercise would be at odds “with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact ... is not enough to prove discrimination,” Chemerinsky contended.

    In her In the Interim column on Monday, Taraleigh Davis revisited comments made by Justice Samuel Alito this fall about the court’s emergency docket, including why it’s so busy these days. The data, according to Davis, “support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the nature of lame-duck confirmations after the showdown between Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, journalists’ records, and weakening the presidential veto.

    Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka continue their discussion on the significance of and fallout from this month’s midterm elections.

    The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

    Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two New Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

    Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, Newly introduced Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

    Woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He swiftly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

    Industry observers note that during the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” New Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

    In 1823, the New Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

    In 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

    Sources indicate that in 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of Latest Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

    Industry observers note that in 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”.

    According to recent reports, in 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of Latest York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

    According to recent reports, woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun noted – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

    Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

    • Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    Sources indicate that in June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

    But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”.

    Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that as Tubi looks to bring more creators to its shores, it is helping them solve a prevalent problem by providing easier access to capital. That’s the gist of the Tubi x Kickstarter Fandom Fund, which unites a Fox-owned streaming service and a 17-year-old crowdfunding platform.

    According to recent reports, the Fandom Fund follows up last year’s FilmStream Collective, a partnership between Tubi and Kickstarter that delivered support to more than 20 independent films. The newly introduced collab between the companies will function similarly; Tubi will throw its weight behind active Kickstarter campaigns, which it will distribute exclusively.

    Tubi won’t just pick any Kickstarter project; instead, as it has done with its other incubator programs, it will hone in on the genres that have the widest appeal among its 110 million monthly active users. The categories fitting that description include horror, YA, Black entertainment, true crime, LGBTQ+, comedy, and reality.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Industry observers note that for Kickstarter, the Fandom Fund represents an increasing commitment to the creator economy. It is part of the three-month-old Culture Fund, which builds on Kickstarter’s enduring status as a key tool for indie artists. In 2024 alone, the platform generated over $700 million of fundraising across more than 35,000 projects.

    Sources indicate that indie creators don’t always get distribution deals with brand-name platforms, but Tubi is eager to support the next generation of storytellers — whom it believes are just as capable as traditional TV voices. To that end, Tubi has premiered a handful of shows and movies led by social media standouts. One of the projects in the Fandom Fund will get a similar treatment by receiving additional backing, allowing it to be developed into a full-length series or feature film.

    “We believe great talent can come from anywhere,” said Tubi GM of Creator Programs and EVP of Business Development Rich Bloom in a statement. “The Fandom Fund gives emerging storytellers the resources to bring those ambitious ideas to life on a bigger canvas while preserving the creative voice, vision and ownership that made their work resonate.”.

    Sources indicate that kickstarter will provide updates about the Fandom Fund through its film-focused newsletter. Participation in the fund requires an active campaign, so if you want Tubi’s backing, get your crowdfunding game on.

    Philips Sonicare Polishes Its Streaming TV Strategy Using Amazon Ads Agent

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brushing your teeth is a chore, and so is trying to buy streaming TV ad inventory publisher by publisher.
    • During the 2025-26 upfront season, Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself.
    • Sources indicate that in both cases, the rationale for consolidation is simplification.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brushing your teeth is a chore, and so is trying to buy streaming TV ad inventory publisher by publisher.

    During the 2025-26 upfront season, Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself. Amazon recently centralized its Amazon DSP has been replaced by a new product called DVA+ (which stands for “display, video and audio”).

    Sources indicate that in both cases, the rationale for consolidation is simplification. When media workflows merge, ad transactions need fewer dashboards and third parties, which improves campaign efficiency and performance.

    Philips Sonicare, which was already using Amazon’s Sponsored Ads to market its products on the flagship site, but wanted to expand its target audience after finding that 86% of the oral care audience segment was not considering Philips products.

    To reach them, the brand paired Amazon’s data with its own first-party data to create custom audience segments of customers who are in market for oral care products but haven’t shopped from Philips before.

    Recent findings suggest that as part of its upfront commitment, Philips used Amazon Ads Agent to buy streaming media across Paramount+, Roku, Tubi, Peacock, TelevisaUnivision and Warner Bros. Discovery. Previously, it had to work with each of these publishers separately.

    By consolidating its buys, Philips saw 24% incremental reach it saw among audiences likely to be interested in its products, as well as a 75% reduction in customer cost per acquisition.

    For brands, centralizing multi-platform streaming buys improves visibility across channels, which helps advertisers learn more about their audience and adjust their campaigns accordingly.

    “By working with Amazon Ads to consolidate our streaming TV investment, we can apply one audience strategy across our portfolio, and manage reach and frequency more effectively while better understanding what happens after an ad is seen,” Priyanti Telang, director of Amazon activation, retail media and digital shelf excellence for Philips North America, told me.

    Using one buying platform also helps Philips speed up reporting.

    Buying media and pulling reports from several platforms is “highly inefficient” because there is audience overlap, said Chris Conetta, director of omnichannel supply for Amazon Ads, so marketers “lose a lot of the incrementality you get when using one tool that can measure audiences across multiple touchpoints.”.

    That logic applies beyond just Amazon’s platform. Amazon (and other retailers, for that matter) can also attract brands seeking more purchase data to improve their performance and attribution, including on streaming TV.

    Since TV is in its performance era, it’s not surprising that Philips was keen to prove streaming’s impact.

    One of the clearest findings from its media consolidation effort, Telang stated, is that “streaming can generate measurable intent.” After seeing the brand’s connected TV ads, more consumers searched online for Philips products by name, she said, and “that intent translated into purchases.”.

    Philips saw a 15x higher purchase rate among consumers who saw the ads on streaming TV than among consumers who only saw a Sponsored Ads placement for Philips online.

    Conetta noted, however, that this increase was a result of customers seeing Philips ads across both streaming and on Amazon’s site. An Amazon executive would say that, but Conetta has a point. Industry research suggests that diversified ad formats can drive improved brand results.

    Philips Sonicare’s experience also says something about streaming TV’s place in the marketing funnel, Telang mentioned, “as a contributor to commercial performance as well as brand awareness.” Guess reach and performance complement each other like brushing and flossing.

    In other words, brace yourselves (ha) to hear more about “full-funnel” advertising in CTV advertising discussions.

    Industry News: Putting AI To Work At WSJ

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The best AI use cases in ad sales aren’t flashy.
    • That’s been the case at The Wall Street Journal, where AI is quietly taking over most of the busywork for the ad sales team, states Josh Stinchcomb, the Journal’s global CRO, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.
    • For example, what seller doesn’t know the frustration of trying to track down a stat buried somewhere in an old email thread or Slack channel when they’re trying to get ready for a meeting?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The best AI use cases in ad sales aren’t flashy. Mostly, it’s about automating the tasks nobody wanted to do anyway.

    That’s been the case at The Wall Street Journal, where AI is quietly taking over most of the busywork for the ad sales team, states Josh Stinchcomb, the Journal’s global CRO, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.

    For example, what seller doesn’t know the frustration of trying to track down a stat buried somewhere in an old email thread or Slack channel when they’re trying to get ready for a meeting?

    Sources indicate that but now, the Journal’s sales team has access to an internal AI-powered search tool that does the digging for them. It can even recap whatever the seller last discussed with a particular prospect so they can walk into their meeting prepared and knowing exactly where the conversation left off.

    “It’s really helpful for pulling from the information we have available to ourselves but isn’t always at our fingertips,” Stinchcomb notes. “That’s been a great time-saver.”.

    There’s also a tool for digital ops that checks line items against ad creative and IOs and also handles taking campaign screenshots, which Stinchcomb describes as a decidedly “laborious and really unfun” task. The result, he notes, is fewer botched campaign debuts and less inventory lost to make-goods.

    But the bigger bet is media planning.

    Right now, it takes a planner four or five hours to turn an RFP into a blueprint, Stinchcomb states, in part because they have to check inventory across multiple different systems. The Journal is testing a tool, however, that can read RFPs, look at past campaigns for similar audiences and build a recommended plan in about an hour.

    Recent findings suggest that with the team producing thousands of plans a year, that’s a lot of hours back in their lives. The time and effort saved is being redeployed toward larger million-dollar-plus RFPs, where Stinchcomb says the Journal’s win rate has gone up five percentage points. A wider rollout of the tool is planned for early next year.

    “Bringing it all together is a great strategy,” he indicates. “It’s an efficient way to bring in chunks of revenue.”.

    But there’s one place where AI isn’t welcome, though, and that’s in the writing of branded content, which is a growing business for the Journal. WSJ Intelligence, its custom content studio, takes its cue from the Journal’s newsroom. The work might be “facilitated by these tools,” Stinchcomb states, “but not written by them.”.

    According to recent reports, “AI is great at sort of rehashing what’s out there,” Stinchcomb claims. “It’s not necessarily great at breaking news, as it were, or bringing a fresher perspective.”.

    Branded content has to be as interesting and engaging as anything else that’s out there competing for a reader’s attention.

    And if it commits the sin of being boring or derivative, Stinchcomb claims, then “[people] don’t read it, and I’m not getting paid.”.

    Also in this episode: Why less than 5% of the Journal’s digital ad revenue is programmatic, how WSJ Intelligence keeps its custom research credible, News Corp’s “woo and sue” approach to AI licensing deals and Stinchcomb’s past life as the singer in a “tragic emo-style” band in high school.

    #8724. Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (882 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Canvas Worldwide’s Agentic Layer Helps Zillow Distinguish Real Renters From Dreamers

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.
    • The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.
    • Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We’ve all been there: You look up a product out of sheer curiosity with no intent to actually spend money on it, and suddenly you’re inundated with ads for similar products.

    The challenge for advertisers is distinguishing the passive browsers from the people with genuine purchase intent.

    Zillow knows that challenge well. Its rental site often serves as a place for people to fantasize about their future home, even if they’re not actually looking to move.

    “We are known for dreaming,” said Ravi Kandikonda, SVP of marketing for Zillow Group. But that’s not necessarily a bad thing. Welcoming the dreamers is a great way for Zillow to drive awareness of its brand and get potential future renters into its platform, Kandikonda added. From there, it’s a matter of striking a balance between building awareness and driving conversions.

    That’s where Zillow turns to its media agency partner, Canvas Worldwide.

    It has been revealed that in September, Canvas declared a new division called ART Dept., which provides a collection of AI solutions to help brands and agencies optimize their campaign budgeting and pacing. Zillow is using ART Dept.’s AI agents to better separate the renters from the dreamers and tailor its marketing accordingly.

    According to recent reports, the “ART” in ART Dept. stands for “AI Applied Research and Technology.” (Though, if we’re being pedantic, wouldn’t that be AART – or AIART?).

    Industry observers note that quibbles about acronyms aside, Canvas’ latest division offers a mix of AI optimization features that are becoming commonplace for ad agencies and marketing platforms. Though, like other agentic platforms, Canvas states its differentiation comes from how it applies those optimizations to its agentic layer.

    For example, offering a pacing dashboard is “table stakes” by now, rather than a distinguishing feature for an agency, said Sally Lee, SVP of programmatic and ART at Canvas.

    But Canvas wanted to make its pacing dashboard “multidimensional” by connecting it with a budget source of truth and building an agentic layer on top of it, stated Lee.

    The agentic layer, called Talos, determines whether a campaign is underpacing or overpacing and optimizes for better performance. Before pushing the newly optimized campaign into the platform, a member of the Canvas team reviews and approves (or denies) it.

    It has been revealed that canvas can “pick and choose from different search and behavioral categories” to optimize against, mentioned Lee. In Zillow’s case, that might include whether a user is researching renter’s insurance or looking into moving truck rentals.

    Canvas gets those behavioral signals through its data partnerships, including its MCP connection to predictive audience targeting company Dstillery.

    Access to behavioral data has helped Zillow reach more specific audiences and be smarter about exactly where and when to target them, stated Kandikonda.

    According to recent reports, for instance, targeting multifamily renters in Seattle using a generic, off-the-shelf “multifamily apartment buildings” audience only goes so far, he noted. “I need to know when they are on a particular platform” to bid for that audience at the right moment with the right content, he added.

    Dstillery’s audience modeling predicts which websites the target audience will visit and when based on real behavioral data. And Canvas’ AI can help surface audience and behavioral overlaps that might have previously gone overlooked by its team.

    Canvas’ reliance on data-backed reasoning was a major draw for Zillow when the two first started working together in 2023, Kandikonda remarked, and it continues to be a major focus of ART Dept.

    The goal behind the new product suite is to save media teams time figuring out what media is performing and how much to spend on different audience segments.

    Increasing ROI is important for any brand. But it’s particularly important within the real estate market, Kandikonda remarked, as marketing dollars are constrained and the entire industry “is bouncing around the box.”.

    So, while Zillow appreciates its dreamer audience, it’s feeling the same pressure most brands are to focus on lower-funnel conversions, such as “actual movers,” Kandikonda mentioned.

    That’s part of the reason off-the-shelf renter audiences weren’t cutting it for Zillow’s ads business, he added.

    An off-the-shelf audience may indicate people who are interested in renting more broadly, he noted, but ART was able to select for people who were actively in the process of planning a move. And more precise targeting means better lower-funnel ad performance.

    The destination, not the journey.

    Industry observers note that from Zillow’s perspective, the biggest change from using Canvas’ ART Dept. is the results, rather than the process. After all, the AI tools are used by the Canvas team, rather than by Zillow.

    Zillow just tells Canvas what outcome it wants to achieve. Canvas then translates the desired outcome into a scorecard that weights different goals and metrics within the interoperable tech infrastructure that powers the ART Dept., which is called +Suite.

    It has been revealed that from there, Canvas’ Audience+ product (which is similar to a data management platform) connects to data partners and the Talos AI agent to build custom audiences. Finally, Talos activates and optimizes the campaign.

    The system creates an ongoing feedback loop, stated Canvas’ Lee: “Build an audience, activate it, see how it’s performing against what that client cares about and identify where to make changes to drive a better outcome.”.

    Only You Can Prevent JavaScript Security Hacks; AppLovin Eyes A Criteo Acquisition

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (904 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.
    • In a recent development, the list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites.
    • “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Adding to the myriad IT outages and cybersecurity scares of the past month, a major malware attack recently hit 178 publications and organizations that use Optimizely’s A/B testing and analytics tools.

    In a recent development, the list included the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, but the problem extends well beyond those high-profile sites. The issue is that many operators don’t audit the tech vendors that drop JavaScript onto their pages.

    “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply-chain attacks, and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators,” Zach Edwards, a researcher for Infoblox and the co-founder of DecryptAds, tells Daniel Krebs of Krebs on Security.

    The “content security policies” (or CSPs) Edwards refers to set limits on what third-party code can do on a site, including what it can load or inject. Of the 178 affected Optimizely accounts, only 24 had CSPs in place and enforced them. Those 24 didn’t spread the malware.

    Because the malware ran in the site’s JavaScript, visitors to pages without CSPs could be infected simply by loading the page – no click or scroll required.

    The main offender, btw, in terms of third-party JavaScript abusers that expose sites to hackers, is ad tech, of course. It’s not even close. Which is why, unfortunately, as Krebs notes, downloading a modern ad blocker is the best solution for consumers to protect themselves.

    The rumor mill is heating up as the year winds down.

    It has been revealed that criteo has been part of that chatter for a while, with private equity firms Vista Equity and Quinti Capital reportedly interested in taking it private. Criteo hasn’t exactly thrived as a public firm, after all.

    But it does possess an immense graph of shopper info.

    It has been revealed that and now another contender has reportedly entered the ring. According to Reuters, AppLovin is among those in talks with Criteo.

    Substantial companies can use deal talks to get an inside look at the finances and operations of smaller companies. Even if the deal doesn’t happen, they’ve still gotten a peek under the hood.

    In a recent development, amazon, for example, was rumored to have considered Criteo once upon a time – not long before launching its own off-site retargeting. Hmm.

    Sources indicate that but Criteo would be an interesting fit for AppLovin. It plugs into a wide network of retailers and web publishers – an entirely upcoming arena to AppLovin, which operates almost entirely in-app – and would bring a large book of business with ecommerce companies. AppLovin has said that it’s a priority to add advertisers to its “consumer” segment, which is primarily ecommerce.

    Criteo would offer a cheat code to get there.

    The rise of residential proxy services that hide bot traffic behind real human IP addresses has been a boon for ad fraud. Often, consumers aren’t even aware they’re acting as a proxy for bot traffic.

    Now, cheap consumer electronics with backdoor vulnerabilities built in can deliver billions of fraudulent ad impressions per day, according to a upcoming report by HUMAN Security’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team.

    The latest scheme Satori uncovered, which it dubbed BADBOX 3.0, was responsible for 40 billion fraudulent bid requests a day at its peak. It used the same residential proxy infrastructure as two other fraud rings that were uncovered by Satori in the past two years – hence the “3.0” branding.

    Industry observers note that the infrastructure relies on cheap TV sets manufactured in China by a tech giant called TXCZ. These TVs have backdoors in their operating systems that allow fraudsters to compromise them.

    Industry observers note that once they’re compromised, the TVs run video ads in the background that the TV owner cannot see. The bid requests for these ads use the TV owner’s IP address to appear as if they’re targeted to a real human. They also impersonate traffic from legitimate CTV apps.

    People who bought one of these TVs pretty much had no chance.

    “It was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers,” notes HUMAN’s Gavin Reid. “Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.”.

    YouTube adjusts its video view counts with modeled co-viewers based on its estimate of how many people saw the screen. [The Verge].

    Netflix is the frontrunner in a bidding war over the broadcast rights for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with experts expecting FIFA to charge up to $2 billion. [The Guardian].

    Recent findings suggest that taylor Swift’s revealed return to the Country Music Awards – her first appearance since 2013 – gave Disney and ABC a chance to squeeze more ad revenue from an event that had already sold out its inventory. [Variety].

    The former editor-in-chief of gaming industry publication Game Developer explains why she recently advised Redditors not to pursue a career in journalism and shares how multiple corporate owners failed to find viable monetization models for the publications she’s worked for since 2006. [ReaderGrev].

    According to recent reports, anthropic priced its initial shares at $83 apiece after demand exceeded expectations. [WSJ].

    Industry observers note that former Jaguar Land Rover North America CMO Charlotte Blank joins behavioral science startup Hive Science as its first-ever chief marketing officer. [MediaPost].

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that pirated content has been an concern for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year.
    • “Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook.
    • Once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that pirated content has been an concern for Meta for so long that it was still known as Facebook when creators first fought back against so-called “freebooters.” To combat unauthorized reuploads, Meta brought a “content protection” tool to Facebook last year. Now, Instagram creators are getting access to that resource as well.

    “Eligible creators” on Instagram can now enroll for access to the management system that was previously limited to Facebook. Like Facebook’s video rights manager, which was itself adapted from previous services like YouTube’s Content ID, the content protection tool uses fingerprinting technology to scan for uploads that are identical to an enrolled creator’s video.

    Once a match is detected, Instagrammers can respond in one of four different ways: They can track the reupload (that’s the default option), request for it to be hidden, require the reuploader to add a credit link, or release their claim on the infringing video. Notably, creators cannot receive monetization through the reposts, as is possible through services like Content ID.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Meta has positioned itself as a champion of original, non-repetitive content. It updated Instagram’s algorithm, providing more visibility for creators who share their own work. Financial penalties for serial reuploaders came to Facebook in 2025, and further penalties arrived on Instagram this year.

    Sources indicate that other platforms have followed Meta’s lead. YouTube cracked down on “mass-produced or repetitive” content in 2025. Earlier this year, Google’s video hub clarified that creators aren’t able to monetize “generic” uploads. Anything “unsatisfying or off-putting” — i.e. the sort of slop you’d expected a generative AI model to spit out — faced similar repercussions.

    Industry observers note that the link between unoriginal reuploads and AI slop is undeniable. Traditional studios have urged platforms to crack down on channels that use AI to steal from artists rather than executing original concepts. Those demands have led to newly introduced rules across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram.

    Recent findings suggest that by bringing content protection to Instagram, Meta is setting itself up to take further action against AI slop in the future. An introductory post explains that “we’re also exploring different ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly,” so stay tuned for that if you’re sick of low-effort AI posts.
